title: Bicycle Race: small two-block codes on the Pareto frontier
abstract: Two-block group-algebra codes are among the simplest quantum LDPC codes, and many of them are translation invariant on a twisted torus, which suits neutral-atom arrays and other platforms with movable qubits. We ask how far they go at small sizes when searched systematically across all groups. To tackle this question, we use a series of algebraic constraints and screens to design a search pipeline capable of enumerating broad and complete swathes of two-block codes on a laptop. With it we census about $10^8$ two-block codes with up to $320$ qubits at check weights five to nine. Several of these censuses are exhaustive, and support complete statements; for instance, the Gross code is, up to equivalence, the only abelian weight-six two-block code with $n \le 200$ to reach $kd^2/n=12$, and the known $[[64,18,8]]$ is the best two-block code by $kd^2/n$ across weights five to nine with $n \le 94$. The censuses are also large enough to give insights into where good codes live - they concentrate in a handful of groups; abelian groups give the best codes at small $n$ and non-abelian groups at large $n$, with the crossover appearing to move out as the check weight grows; and high quality codes become $100$ to $1000$ times rarer per draw from weight six to weights eight and nine. Using the group algebra and the census data to steer a statistical search finds four to fifteen times as many good codes as uniform draws in equal time. Among the codes found are $[[102,20,10]]$ and $[[120,24,10]]$ at check weight nine, which we simulate in noisy syndrome-extraction circuits, and $[[288,16,16]]$, the best weight-six two-block code with $n \le 300$. At check weights seven to nine, our best codes exceed the best published $kd^2/n$ with exact distance at the same check weight in most length bands up to $320$ qubits. All codes are available in a public database.
summary: This paper performs an exhaustive, systematic search for optimal two-block quantum LDPC codes, analyzing their performance across various physical sizes and check weights. By developing specialized search pipelines, the authors establish new state-of-the-art performance records for key metrics like $kd^2/n$. The results are highly relevant for experimental quantum computing platforms, particularly those utilizing neutral atoms.
main_problem: The paper systematically searches for and characterizes high-performing two-block quantum LDPC codes to map out their performance on the Pareto frontier.
main_result: The authors census numerous two-block codes, setting new records for the $kd^2/n$ metric compared to published literature across various check weights and physical sizes up to 320 qubits.
method: The methodology involves designing an algebraic search pipeline using constraints to enumerate codes, followed by comparing performance metrics like $kd^2/n$ against established theoretical bounds.
model_or_system: The focus is on two-block group-algebra codes, which are a specific, simple class of quantum LDPC codes suitable for implementation on platforms like neutral-atom arrays.
key_observables: Code parameters $(n, k, d)$ and performance metrics such as $kd^2/n$, $d/n$, and $n/k$.
important_parameters: Check weights (specifically 5 through 9), physical qubit size ($n \le 320$), and the group structure (abelian vs. non-abelian).
main_assumptions: The search is computationally limited to $n \le 320$ and check weights up to nine; the analysis compares results against existing literature bounds.
figures_summary: Figures systematically plot the Pareto fronts and performance metrics ($d$ vs $n$, $kd^2/n$ vs $n$) for various check weights, comparing the authors' results against literature bounds.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the search space, presenting exhaustive censuses for specific constraints (e.g., weight-six codes), and then systematically comparing the best found codes against established theoretical and experimental bounds across multiple figures and tables.
why_interesting: The explicit mention of suitability for neutral-atom arrays and movable qubits directly connects the abstract theory of quantum error correction to current, leading-edge experimental platforms in AMO physics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Figure 2: The search pipeline. Top: the outer loop. A target (check weight and n band) is first sampled uniformly over groups and block pairs; we then return to theory to try to explain what the good codes have in common. Later rounds then sample toward those structures. Bottom: every candidate (G, a, b) is reduced up to equivalence, screened with cheap bounds on k and d, and given a distance, witnesses first and exact for the survivors; the results are compared with the literature and may feed the next round.
